method_rationale: Both proteins are plasma-membrane receptors that HPA places in lymphoid tissue, and GPR174 is enriched in T and NK cells. The prediction is a cis interaction on the same cell, so in situ proximity detection (<40 nm) fits better than a stimulation assay, because neither protein is a secreted ligand. PLA also avoids detergent solubilisation of a GPCR and a cytokine receptor, which co-IP would require.
tissue_rationale: HPA lists lymphoid tissue as the tissue-specific RNA site for both proteins (IL12RB1 22.7 nTPM, GPR174 15.7 nTPM), so this is the one tissue where both are clearly expressed. HPA single-cell data show GPR174 highest in T-cells (105 nCPM) and NK-cells (76 nCPM), with thymocytes at 38. These are also the cells where IL12RB1 is expected to be functionally relevant. I chose lymph node, tonsil, spleen and thymus as lymphoid tissue sources; this is my inference, since the HPA data provided give only the "lymphoid tissue" grouping.
protocol_notes:
1) Use primary human T and NK cells, ideally after IL-2 or anti-CD3/CD28 activation to induce IL12RB1. Add a Jurkat or NK-92 line as a secondary system. Fix gently with 2–4% PFA without permeabilisation, so that only surface epitopes are detected. Also test FFPE tonsil or lymph node sections.
2) Run Duolink PLA with a mouse anti-IL12RB1 and a rabbit anti-GPR174 that target extracellular regions. Validate each antibody first by IF/flow on overexpressing versus knockout or knockdown cells. Co-stain CD3 or CD56 and a membrane marker to assign the PLA puncta to cell type and to the plasma membrane. Quantify puncta per cell by confocal imaging.
3) Run a parallel PLA with IL12RB1 against IL12RB2 or IL23R. Also test whether IL-12 or IL-23 stimulation (15–30 min) changes the IL12RB1–GPR174 PLA signal, to see whether the interaction depends on the receptor complex. Add a GPR174 ligand (lysophosphatidylserine) condition to test whether ligand engagement modulates proximity.
4) Confirm orthogonally with HEK293 co-transfection and co-IP, then a functional readout such as pSTAT4 by flow with and without GPR174 knockout.
controls: Positive: IL12RB1–IL12RB2 or IL12RB1–IL23R PLA, or a known abundant same-cell surface pair such as CD3–TCR. Negative: single-antibody and no-primary-antibody PLA controls. Also use GPR174 CRISPR-knockout or siRNA-knockdown T cells, IL12RB1-knockout cells, and an irrelevant membrane receptor not expected to interact with IL12RB1 (for example CD45 or a different GPCR). Include an isotype-matched IgG PLA pair. For the expression-dependence control, use a cell line lacking both proteins, then transfect each protein alone and together.
caveats: AF3 ipTM is only 0.58, so the model is low confidence. Both proteins are glycoproteins and I could not place the glycosylation sites relative to the predicted interface, so a glycan may block or gate the contact in cells. This pair is not flagged LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM, but a glycosidase arm (PNGase F) is a reasonable follow-up if the first PLA is negative. IL12RB1 normally acts with IL12RB2 or IL23R, which were not in the model, so the real interaction may need those subunits or be competed by them. PLA shows proximity only (<40 nm), not direct binding, and crowded T-cell membranes can give false positives. HPA provides no protein-level data for either gene here, only RNA, so antibody availability and protein expression must be checked. Surface expression of IL12RB1 on resting T cells is low.

method_rationale: Both are membrane proteins expected in the same immune cell, and the hypothesis is a cis interaction in one membrane. PLA tests in-situ proximity (<40 nm) in native membranes without detergent solubilisation. Detergent could break or create GPCR/TM-helix associations, so co-IP is less suitable. Neither protein is a secreted ligand, so a stimulation assay doesn't fit.
tissue_rationale: Both show RNA in bone marrow and lymphoid tissue (LAIR1 lymphoid 44.5 nTPM; GPR65 bone marrow 11.9 and lymphoid 9.1 nTPM). LAIR1 protein is high in bone marrow, lymphoid tissue and lung. Lung is included as a LAIR1 protein-positive tissue that also contains mast cells (GPR65 single-cell peak, 495 nCPM), but GPR65 expression there is not shown in the data given.
protocol_notes: 1) Use a cell system that expresses both proteins, such as human mast cell lines (LAD2, HMC-1), primary monocytes/T cells, or tonsil/lymph node sections. Add a HEK293 model with tagged LAIR1 and GPR65 for antibody validation and clean positive/negative arms. 2) Use mild fixation (4% PFA, no permeabilisation or only light permeabilisation) with a mouse anti-LAIR1 extracellular-domain antibody and a rabbit anti-GPR65 antibody. Use species-matched PLA probes, and add anti-tag antibodies in the HEK293 model if the endogenous antibodies are poor. 3) GPR65 is annotated as vesicular in HPA, so co-stain for the plasma membrane (e.g. WGA or CD45) and an endosome marker (EEA1 or LAMP1). Quantify PLA dots per cell at the surface versus in vesicles. 4) Run a pH series (7.4 vs 6.5), since GPR65 is a proton-sensing receptor, and check whether LAIR1 crosslinking with collagen or an agonist antibody changes the signal.
controls: Positive: a known LAIR1-proximal pair (LAIR1 with SHP-1 or with itself, via two LAIR1 antibodies) and a known GPR65 partner or a GPR65 homodimer pair. Negative: single-antibody PLA, PLA in LAIR1 or GPR65 CRISPR-KO or siRNA cells, and LAIR1 with an unrelated abundant membrane protein (e.g. CD45 or an unrelated GPCR) to check for crowding artifacts. Extra specificity control: HEK293 cells expressing only one partner, or each partner co-expressed with an unrelated single-TM protein and an unrelated GPCR.
caveats: Confidence is low: ipTM 0.58, GPR65 pLDDT 53.5, and a very large interface (4476 Å2) that is probably non-specific packing of LAIR1's single TM helix against the GPCR bundle, which AF3 produces without a bilayer. A positive PLA only shows proximity, and abundant membrane proteins can give false positives. LAIR1 (1 N-glycan site) and GPR65 (3 sites) are glycoproteins, and I did not check whether those sites lie on the modelled interface. Glycans could block the interface, so the AF3 pose is not guaranteed in vivo. If PLA is positive, test for a glycan role with PNGase F/Endo H treatment or glycan-site mutants. GPR65 is mainly vesicular in HPA, so it may not meet LAIR1 at the plasma membrane. HPA gives no GPR65 protein-level data, and mast cells are not among LAIR1's listed cell types (microglia), so the cell-level overlap is uncertain. Antibody quality is also a risk.

method_variant: Recombinant CCL11 on GPR132-expressing vs. parental cells, with CCR3 as a positive control for CCL11 and a glycosidase/glycosylation-site mutant arm
method_rationale: CCL11 is a secreted chemokine and GPR132 is a 7-TM GPCR, so this is a paracrine ligand-receptor pair. A functional readout (G-protein/β-arrestin signalling) tests whether CCL11 activates GPR132 and is more informative than co-localization. HPA gives no tissue-level GPR132 data, so a PLA in tissue isn't feasible.
target_tissues: Blood (CCL11 secretome location: secreted to blood)
Immune cells such as macrophages and eosinophils (GPR132 candidate side; to be confirmed experimentally)
tissue_rationale: HPA gives no tissue-level RNA or protein specificity for either gene. The only expression data is CCL11 RNA in fibroblasts (44.2 nCPM), and CCL11 is annotated as secreted to blood. There is no real overlap, so the assay uses a recombinant ligand or fibroblast co-culture on a receptor-expressing cell. GPR132 expression in the responder cells must be verified by qPCR first.
cell_types: Macrophages or other immune cells endogenously expressing GPR132
protocol_notes:
1) Generate HEK293 (or CHO) cells stably expressing tagged GPR132 and parental or empty-vector controls. Confirm surface expression by FLAG/HA staining. Add a CCR3-expressing line as a CCL11 positive control.
2) Stimulate with recombinant human CCL11 (dose range 1 nM–1 µM, 5–60 min). Read out Gi/Gq/Gs signalling (cAMP, Ca2+ flux, or IP1), β-arrestin recruitment (e.g. PathHunter/BRET), and ERK phosphorylation. Optionally measure transwell chemotaxis.
3) Test fibroblast-conditioned medium or co-culture, with a CCL11-neutralizing antibody or CCL11 knockdown as a specificity control.
4) Run a binding check (e.g. fluorescent CCL11 binding or a BRET ligand-binding assay) to separate direct binding from indirect effects. Include the glycosidase arm described in the variant.
controls: Positive: CCL11 on CCR3-expressing cells (calcium flux, chemotaxis). Positive for GPR132 function: its known agonist 9-HODE, or acidic pH/proton stimulation. Negative: parental or empty-vector cells, heat-denatured CCL11, an unrelated chemokine (e.g. CCL2), a CCR3 antagonist to rule out endogenous CCR3 signalling, and a GPR132-knockout or siRNA arm in endogenous cells.
caveats: Confidence is low: ipTM 0.56 and p_twoway 0.0499 are only marginally above threshold. CCL11's established receptor is CCR3, and GPR132 is known as a receptor for oxidized fatty acids and protons. Any signal could therefore come from endogenous CCR3/ACKR receptors or from pH effects of the buffer, so control the buffer pH. Both proteins have one glycosylation site, and its position relative to the modeled interface was not checked. AF3 may have modeled a bare-sequence interface that a glycan blocks in reality, so a negative result in glycosylated protein, or a positive result only without glycan, would be informative. HPA lists GPR132 as 'predicted intracellular', and it has no tissue or cell-type RNA data, so confirm surface localization and endogenous expression.

method_variant: Recombinant PPIA (+/- CsA/PPIA catalytic-dead R55A, +/- CCL5 and BSG co-stimulation) on GPR75-expressing vs GPR75-knockout cells, with a PNGase F/glycosylation-site mutant arm as a secondary check
method_rationale: PPIA is secreted to blood and GPR75 is a plasma-membrane GPCR, so this is an extracellular ligand-receptor hypothesis. A functional GPCR readout is more informative than co-localization for this pair. GPR75 is known to couple to Gq/11 (CCL5 and 20-HETE signalling), so calcium and IP1 readouts are plausible.
tissue_rationale: GPR75 RNA is tissue-enriched only in brain (9.8 nTPM) and retina (7.1 nTPM). PPIA is a housekeeping protein with very high, near-ubiquitous expression (e.g. 3194 nCPM in gastric progenitor cells) and is secreted to blood, so PPIA is available wherever GPR75 is. There is no tissue-specific PPIA restriction, so the receptor side determines the tissue choice. For the assay, use GPR75-expressing cells such as HEK293 transfectants, plus a brain/retina-derived line or primary cells, with recombinant PPIA supplied exogenously.
protocol_notes:
1) Use HEK293 cells stably expressing tagged GPR75 (HA- or FLAP-tagged, to confirm surface expression) and parental or GPR75-KO cells as the control. Optionally add a neuronal or RPE line with endogenous GPR75 (confirm by qPCR). Add a Gq-proximal readout: Fluo-4 calcium flux, IP-One HTRF, or NFAT-luciferase, plus ERK1/2 phosphorylation by western blot at 2-30 min.
2) Dose-response of endotoxin-free recombinant human PPIA (1 nM-10 µM), with heat-denatured PPIA as a protein control. Test CCL5 as a positive control for GPR75 activation. Test whether BSG/CD147 is required, by BSG knockdown or anti-CD147 blocking antibody, since PPIA signals via BSG and may produce a GPR75-independent response.
3) Confirm physical binding orthogonally: surface binding of biotin- or fluorophore-labelled PPIA to GPR75+ vs GPR75-KO cells by flow cytometry, or SPR/BLI with purified GPR75 or membrane preparations. Use cyclosporin A and PPIA R55A to test whether the isomerase active site is involved.
controls: Positive: CCL5 (reported GPR75 ligand) and a Gq agonist such as carbachol or ATP for the assay window. Negative: parental/GPR75-KO cells, heat-denatured PPIA, an unrelated cyclophilin (PPIB), a GPCR-unrelated receptor-expressing line, and vehicle. For specificity, include an anti-CD147 blocking arm and a CsA arm.
caveats: AF3 support is modest (ipTM 0.56, interface pLDDT 68.2), so the predicted interface may not be real. PPIA is an abundant hub with 195 known interactions, so non-specific binding is likely, and recombinant PPIA at high concentration can act through BSG/CD147 or other routes. GPR75 has 3 glycosylation sites, and their position relative to the predicted interface was not checked. Glycans could occlude or alter the interface, so run a glycosylation-site mutant (N-to-Q) or PNGase F arm for interpretation. The HPA data give no protein-level tissue data for either protein. GPR75 is a poorly characterised, low-expressed receptor, and antibodies and surface expression may be difficult. The proposed CCL5 and BSG partners are candidate co-factors, not confirmed members of a complex.

method_variant: Compare full-length C3, C3b/iC3b/C3a/C3c/C3d fragments (and optionally PNGase F-deglycosylated C3) on GPR174-expressing vs GPR174-knockout cells, with LysoPS as a reference agonist.
method_rationale: C3 is a secreted plasma protein and GPR174 is a plasma-membrane GPCR on lymphocytes, so this is a paracrine/endocrine ligand-receptor pair. Cells need not co-express them, and a signalling readout tests function better than co-localization. GPR174 couples to Gs, so cAMP and pCREB are the plausible readouts.
tissue_rationale: There is no real tissue overlap. C3 RNA is almost entirely liver (5062 nTPM, hepatocytes 5036 nCPM) and reaches the receptor through blood. GPR174 RNA is restricted to lymphoid tissue (15.7 nTPM), with the highest single-cell levels in T-cells (105 nCPM), NK-cells (76) and basophils (60). Lymphocytes are therefore the receptor-bearing side, bathed in plasma C3 (liver-derived).
protocol_notes:
1) Use HEK293 (or CHO) cells stably expressing GPR174, with a CRE-luciferase or cAMP biosensor (GloSensor/HTRF cAMP). Use parental or empty-vector cells as the negative control. Confirm in primary human CD4+ T cells or Jurkat cells, with GPR174 knocked out by CRISPR, by measuring cAMP, pCREB (Ser133) and inhibition of TCR-induced proliferation or IL-2.
2) Treat with a dose range (1 nM–10 µM) of purified native human C3, C3b, iC3b, C3a, C3c and C3d, and with Hep G2 conditioned medium or co-culture as a physiological C3 source. Include a time course (5–60 min for cAMP, 4–6 h for the reporter).
3) Orthogonal binding check: use SPR or a cell-binding assay with tagged C3 on GPR174+ vs GPR174− cells, plus a β-arrestin recruitment assay (e.g. PathHunter) in case signalling is Gs-independent.
4) Run a glycosylation arm: PNGase F or Endo H pre-treated C3, and an N-glycan-site mutant of GPR174 if the interface overlaps a site. Test whether the response is lost, gained or unchanged.
controls: Positive: LysoPS (the established GPR174 agonist), and forskolin for the maximal cAMP response. Negative: parental or GPR174-KO cells, heat-denatured C3, and an irrelevant plasma protein such as albumin at the same concentration. Specificity: C3a on C3AR1-expressing cells as a reference, and a C3AR1/C5AR2 co-expression arm to test whether the other subunits modulate the response. Also check LysoPS contamination, since lipid carry-over in plasma-derived C3 could give a false signal. Use delipidated C3 or recombinant C3.
caveats: Confidence is low (ipTM 0.55, interface pLDDT 68.7, min PAE 9.1). The AF3 model used the uncleaved full-length C3 precursor, which does not exist in plasma, so the real binder may be a cleavage fragment (C3a, C3b, iC3b, C3d) or none. GPR174's known ligand is a lipid (LysoPS), so a peptide/protein interface is unprecedented. Plasma-purified C3 may carry lipids that activate GPR174 and give false positives. Glycosylation sites on C3 and GPR174 were not checked against the predicted interface, so a glycan could block or alter binding. GPR174 expression is modest (RNA only, no HPA protein data), and the C3AR1/C5AR2 co-subunits could confound the readouts. If no signal appears, consider that C3 may bind without activating (a modulator or antagonist), and follow up with co-IP or a binding assay.

method_variant: with GPR141 knockdown/knockout and single-antibody controls; optionally a C5a-stimulated vs. unstimulated arm
method_rationale: Both are 7TM GPCRs expected in the same cell membrane, and the question is whether they sit in close proximity as a heterodimer. PLA tests this in situ in primary myeloid cells at endogenous expression levels. Neither protein is a secreted ligand, so a stimulation assay is not the primary fit.
tissue_rationale: Bone marrow is the only tissue where both are reported. C5AR1 has very high protein intensity there, and GPR141 RNA is 24.5 nTPM. At single-cell level, C5AR1 is high in neutrophils (2004 nCPM) and monocytes (1283 nCPM), and GPR141 is detected in neutrophil progenitors (17.8 nCPM). The overlap is therefore the neutrophil lineage.
protocol_notes: 1) Use bone marrow sections or cytospins of CD34+-derived, differentiating neutrophil-lineage cells (e.g. HL-60 or PLB-985 differentiated toward neutrophils, plus primary bone marrow cells). GPR141 expression is low and is likely restricted to progenitors, so sample the differentiation time course. 2) Use PLA with a validated anti-C5AR1 (e.g. mouse mAb) and an anti-GPR141 (rabbit). Validate the GPR141 antibody first by western blot or immunofluorescence on GPR141-overexpressing versus knockout cells, because it is an orphan with little antibody validation. Use mild fixation (4% PFA) and avoid permeabilisation that disrupts the membrane. 3) Quantify PLA puncta per cell by confocal microscopy and compare with the controls. Run a follow-up with HEK293 cells co-expressing tagged receptors (e.g. NanoBRET or co-IP) to confirm the specificity of the interaction. 4) Optionally test whether C5a changes the PLA signal and whether GPR141 modulates C5a-induced Gi signalling (cAMP, Ca2+ flux) given the GNAI1/GNAO1 partners.
controls: Positive: C5AR1 with a known interactor or a known GPCR homodimer pair (e.g. C5AR1 with C5AR2, or CXCR4 with CXCR4) to show PLA works for GPCR dimers. Negative: single-primary-antibody PLA, GPR141 CRISPR KO or siRNA cells, C5AR1 with an unrelated abundant membrane protein (e.g. CD45), and C5AR1 with a non-myeloid GPCR that is not expressed in the same cells. Also a mixed-cell control: C5AR1-only and GPR141-only cells mixed together, which should give no PLA signal.
caveats: Confidence is low: ipTM is 0.54, interface pLDDT is about 71, and AF3 may pack 7TM bundles together without a bilayer, so a non-specific association is possible. HPA lists the main location of C5AR1 as Golgi, which probably reflects antibody or biosynthetic-pool staining rather than its functional plasma-membrane location. GPR141 has no HPA localization or protein data and its RNA level is low, so the PLA signal may be near background and antibody specificity is the main risk. Overlap is in bone marrow neutrophil lineage cells only, and GPR141 appears restricted to progenitors, where C5AR1 may be lower. PLA detects proximity of about 40 nm, so crowded receptors in the same membrane can give false positives. Positive results need a second orthogonal method (co-IP or BRET).

method_variant: Compare WT RNASET2 vs catalytically dead RNASET2 (H65F/H69F) and, optionally, PNGase F/EndoH-deglycosylated or N-glycan site mutant RNASET2 to test glycan dependence of the interface.
method_rationale: RNASET2 is a secreted protein and GPR82 is an orphan cell-surface GPCR, so the natural test is whether recombinant RNASET2 activates GPR82-expressing cells. A functional readout also distinguishes true agonism from non-specific binding, which matters given the borderline ipTM of 0.54.
tissue_rationale: GPR82 RNA is highest in lymphoid tissue (6.5 nTPM) and intestine (2.5 nTPM), and its single-cell signal is in Kupffer cells (65.1 nCPM), so liver macrophages and lymphoid immune cells are the receptor-bearing side. RNASET2 is secreted to blood and is very high in endometrial luminal cells (742 nCPM). There is no clear tissue overlap, so this is a paracrine/endocrine pairing and is best tested by adding ligand to receptor-bearing cells (co-culture or recombinant protein).
protocol_notes: 1) Use HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing tagged GPR82 (e.g. N-terminal HA/FLAG) and parental cells as a control. Add recombinant human RNASET2 (mammalian-expressed, glycosylated) at 1 nM–1 µM. Measure cAMP, because GPR82 is reported to be constitutively active and probably Gi/Gs-coupled (GloSensor or HTRF, with forskolin to detect Gi inhibition). Also run a β-arrestin recruitment assay (PathHunter/NanoBiT) and a Ca2+ flux assay with Gα16/Gqi5 co-expression. 2) Confirm binding with a cell-surface binding assay: tagged RNASET2 on GPR82+ vs parental cells by flow cytometry. 3) Confirm in a physiological system: stimulate primary human macrophages or Kupffer-like cells (or THP-1/PBMC-derived macrophages) with RNASET2, with and without GPR82 siRNA/CRISPR knockout, and read out cAMP or ERK phosphorylation. Alternatively co-culture with RNASET2-secreting endometrial epithelial cells such as Ishikawa cells, with RNASET2 knockdown. 4) Run the glycosylation arm: PNGase F-treated or N-glycan-site mutant RNASET2 against WT.
controls: Positive: a known agonist or assay-validation ligand for a co-expressed control GPCR (e.g. forskolin for cAMP, or a known ligand of an unrelated receptor in the same cell background). Negative: parental cells lacking GPR82; an irrelevant secreted RNase (e.g. RNase A/RNASE T1) or heat-denatured RNASET2; a mock-transfected receptor such as another orphan GPCR (GPR84 or GPR34); buffer-only vehicle. Also include catalytically dead RNASET2 to separate RNase activity from receptor engagement.
caveats: The ipTM of 0.54 is borderline, so the predicted interface is low confidence. Both proteins carry N-glycosylation sites (RNASET2 has 3, GPR82 has 2), and their position relative to the modeled interface has not been checked. The AF3 bare-sequence model could therefore be blocked or altered by glycans, so use glycosylated, mammalian-expressed recombinant protein and test the deglycosylated version. HPA has no subcellular data for either protein, and GPR82 has low RNA expression, so antibody availability is uncertain and native-cell responses may be small. GPR82 is orphan and constitutively active, so a ligand effect may be subtle (inverse agonism or modulation). RNASET2 also has RNase-dependent and independent activities, which could produce receptor-independent effects on cells. RNASET2 is annotated as both predicted intracellular and secreted, so confirm its secretion in the chosen cells.

method_variant: Include BSG/CD147-knockout or CD147-blocking antibody arm, and a PNGase F/tunicamycin arm to test GPR82 glycan role
method_rationale: PPIA is a secreted extracellular ligand (HPA: secreted to blood) and GPR82 is an orphan membrane GPCR, so the two do not need to be in the same cell. A functional readout (G-protein/β-arrestin signalling) on receptor-expressing cells tests whether PPIA actually engages GPR82, which a co-localisation read cannot show.
tissue_rationale: GPR82 RNA is enriched in lymphoid tissue (6.5 nTPM) and intestine (2.5 nTPM), and in Kupffer cells (65.1 nCPM). PPIA is highly expressed, e.g. 3194 nCPM in gastric progenitor cells, and circulates in blood, so intestinal epithelium can supply the ligand locally while lymphoid and Kupffer cells provide the receptor. The expression overlap is therefore paracrine rather than same-cell. Liver is named only for the Kupffer-cell single-cell signal.
protocol_notes: 1) Use HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing tagged GPR82, with parental cells as the control. Optionally add a monocyte/macrophage line or primary Kupffer-like macrophages with endogenous GPR82 (confirm by qPCR). Treat with recombinant human PPIA (1 nM–1 µM, 5–60 min). Read out cAMP (GPR82 is reported to be Gi/constitutively active, so use forskolin-stimulated cAMP), a β-arrestin recruitment assay (e.g. PathHunter/NanoBiT), and pERK. Use a GPR82-orphan-compatible Gα16 or Gqi5 chimera calcium flux as a secondary readout. 2) Test dependence on BSG: use BSG-KO cells or an anti-CD147 blocking antibody, and add BSG co-expression, since the pair is flagged with BSG as another subunit. Also test whether PPIA binding is blocked by cyclosporin A, which occupies the PPIA active site. 3) As orthogonal binding evidence, run flow cytometry or a cell-surface binding assay with tagged PPIA on GPR82-expressing versus parental cells, and run a pull-down with PPIA on membrane preparations.
controls: Positive: a known GPCR agonist in the assay system (e.g. forskolin for the cAMP window; PPIA on CD147-expressing cells for the known PPIA–BSG pathway, e.g. ERK activation or chemotaxis). Negative: parental or empty-vector cells; heat-denatured PPIA or a PPIA catalytic-dead mutant (R55A); an unrelated cyclophilin (PPIB) or another secreted protein; an unrelated GPCR expressed at equal surface levels; pertussis toxin to test Gi dependence.
caveats: Confidence is low (ipTM 0.53). PPIA is an abundant hub protein with 195 known interactions, so a hit could be nonspecific or act through its known receptor BSG/CD147 rather than GPR82 directly. HPA gives no subcellular data for either protein, and I could not check which side of the membrane the modeled interface sits on, or whether GPR82 N-glycosylation sites fall on the interface. If a glycan blocks the interface, the bare-sequence AF3 model would not match reality, hence the deglycosylation/glycosylation-site mutant arm. GPR82 RNA is low in bulk tissue (2.5–6.5 nTPM) and there is no protein-level HPA data, so a recombinant overexpression system is needed. Surface expression of tagged GPR82 and the lack of a validated antibody should be confirmed. Endogenous PPIA in conditioned medium may mask the response, so wash the cells or use serum-free medium.

method_variant: Include a binding arm: biotinylated or tagged recombinant CCL28 on GPRC5A-overexpressing vs. knockout cells (flow cytometry), plus an optional PNGase F / N-glycan site mutant arm for GPRC5A and CCL28.
method_rationale: CCL28 is a secreted chemokine (secreted to blood) and GPRC5A is an orphan class C GPCR, so the pair is a ligand/receptor candidate. HPA shows the two proteins expressed in different tissues, which fits a paracrine stimulation assay with recombinant ligand better than in situ proximity. A functional readout also tests whether binding does anything, which matters because chemokines can dock non-specifically into GPCR bundles.
tissue_rationale: HPA shows GPRC5A RNA enriched in lung (190 nTPM) and urinary bladder (122 nTPM), with lung protein detected. CCL28 RNA is enriched in salivary gland (283 nTPM), and in salivary and lacrimal acinar cells (about 1260 and 1400 nCPM). The two proteins have no real tissue overlap: the receptor-bearing side is lung/bladder epithelium and the ligand-producing side is salivary/lacrimal acinar cells. Because CCL28 is secreted to blood and mucosal fluids, it can plausibly reach lung epithelium, so use recombinant CCL28 or salivary-acinar-conditioned medium on lung epithelial cells.
cell_types: Lung epithelial cells (alveolar type II / bronchial epithelial)
protocol_notes:
1) Use a GPRC5A-high lung epithelial line (e.g. BEAS-2B, or A549 if expression is confirmed by qPCR/WB) and a CRISPR GPRC5A-KO isogenic line. Also use HEK293 cells with and without GPRC5A overexpression. Confirm that CCR3/CCR10 are low or absent, or block them with antagonists or knock them out, so the response is not read through the known CCL28 receptors.
2) Stimulate with recombinant human CCL28 (10–500 nM dose-response, 5–60 min). Read out Gi/cAMP (forskolin-induced cAMP, or a BRET sensor), ERK1/2 and Src-family/STAT3 phosphorylation by western or AlphaLISA, β-arrestin recruitment (NanoBiT/Tango), and receptor internalization. GPRC5A localises to vesicles, so image its trafficking after stimulation. Also run a transwell migration assay as a functional readout.
3) Run a direct binding arm: tagged CCL28 on GPRC5A+ vs. KO cells by flow cytometry. Add a competition arm with excess untagged CCL28 and a heparin/GAG-stripping control, because CCL28 is highly basic and sticks non-specifically to cell-surface GAGs.
4) For the glycan check, treat cells or ligand with PNGase F, or mutate the predicted N-glycosylation sites on GPRC5A and CCL28 (N→Q), and compare the response with wild type.
controls: Positive: CCL28 on CCR10- or CCR3-expressing cells (e.g. CCR10-transfected cells, with Ca2+ flux or migration readout), which confirms the ligand is active. Negative: GPRC5A-KO or parental cells lacking GPRC5A, heat-denatured CCL28, an irrelevant chemokine (e.g. CCL21) and a different class C GPCR (e.g. GPRC5B). Also use a CCL28 binding-interface mutant if the AF3 model suggests one, and pertussis toxin to test Gi dependence.
caveats: Low confidence: the AF3 ipTM of 0.53 is borderline, and chemokines often dock non-specifically into GPCR bundles. CCL28 is very basic and binds cell-surface GAGs, so binding must be tested against GAG-stripped and KO controls. HPA lists GPRC5A mainly in vesicles (and also as predicted intracellular), so surface exposure is uncertain and the extracellular accessibility of the modeled interface needs confirming (surface biotinylation or non-permeabilized staining). GPRC5A is an orphan receptor with weak canonical G-protein coupling, so the signalling readout may be negative even if binding occurs. One N-glycosylation site on each protein has not been checked against the interface, so a glycan could block the AF3 bare-sequence interface. The glycosidase/mutant arm addresses this. HPA shows no tissue overlap of the two proteins, so any physiological relevance would be endocrine or paracrine, via mucosal secretion or blood.

method_variant: Include MST1R-null/MST1R-blocked arm and a GPR37 vs vector-only arm to separate direct GPR37 signalling from MST1R-mediated effects
method_rationale: MST1 (HGF-like protein, MSP) is a secreted-to-blood ligand and GPR37 is a GPCR, so this is an endocrine ligand-receptor pair with no expected same-cell co-expression. A functional readout in receptor-expressing cells fits better than PLA. Because MST1R is named as another subunit, the assay must separate GPR37 effects from canonical MST1R signalling.
tissue_rationale: MST1 RNA is almost exclusively hepatic (liver 864 nTPM; hepatocytes 369 nCPM). GPR37 is in brain (67 nTPM; cerebral cortex protein intensity ~1.08M) and retina (36 nTPM). There is no real tissue overlap, so this would be endocrine signalling from liver to CNS/retina. Test it with recombinant MST1 on GPR37-expressing cells, not in a shared tissue.
protocol_notes: 1) Receptor cells: HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing GPR37 (with and without MST1R), plus a vector-only control. Also test primary oligodendrocyte precursors or Müller glia/oligodendrocyte-lineage lines, which express GPR37 endogenously. 2) Stimulate with recombinant human MST1 (active, two-chain form, ~1–500 nM dose-response; 5–60 min). Active MST1 needs proteolytic cleavage, so compare pro-MST1 with the cleaved form, or use conditioned medium from HepG2 or hepatocytes. 3) Readouts: cAMP (GloSensor), β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter/BRET), Ca2+ flux, and pERK1/2 and pAKT by western blot. Use MST1R signalling (pERK, pMET-like phosphorylation) as a reference. 4) Confirm binding orthogonally with a cell-surface binding assay (tagged MST1 on GPR37 cells, flow cytometry) or by co-IP/pulldown. Use an MST1R siRNA or blocking antibody to dissect dependence.
controls: Positive: MST1 on MST1R-expressing cells (e.g. macrophages or MST1R-HEK) gives pERK/pRON. For GPR37, use the known ligands prosaposin/prosaptide (TX14(A)) or head activator. Negative: untransfected or vector-only cells, heat-inactivated MST1, an unrelated HGF-family protein (HGF), and a GPR37L1-expressing line for specificity. Verify GPR37 surface expression, for example with an N-terminal tag.
caveats: Low confidence: ipTM 0.52, p_twoway 0.050, and the pair has no support in STRING, CellPhoneDB or the literature. The GPR37 N-terminus is heavily glycosylated, and the glycosylation could not be checked against the interface. GPR37 also misfolds and is retained intracellularly (HPA lists nuclear membrane), so surface expression in heterologous cells may be poor. The MST1 UniProt lookup returned STK4 (Q13043), so MST1 has no valid PTM or mechanism data. MST1 is also activated by proteolytic cleavage, which the AF3 model may not reflect. Any response could come via MST1R, so the MST1R arms are needed to interpret it. Tissue separation means any in vivo relevance would be endocrine and would have to cross the blood-brain or blood-retina barrier.

method_variant: Include a B2M-knockdown/exogenous recombinant B2M add-back arm and a heavy-chain (HLA-ABC) co-stain to distinguish free B2M from MHC-I-bound B2M
method_rationale: B2M is ubiquitously expressed on cell surfaces and also circulates, while GPR82 is a plasma-membrane orphan GPCR with no known ligand, so there is no established signalling readout. PLA detects surface proximity in situ. A ligand-style stimulation assay is not suitable because there is no validated GPR82 readout, and orphan GPCR coupling is uncertain.
tissue_rationale: GPR82 RNA is highest in lymphoid tissue (6.5 nTPM) and intestine (2.5 nTPM). Its single-cell expression is enriched in Kupffer cells (65.1 nCPM). B2M is secreted to blood and is also on the plasma membrane of nearly all nucleated cells, so it overlaps wherever GPR82 is present. HPA gives no tissue-specific B2M numbers, so this overlap is inferred from B2M's broad expression.
cell_types: Lymphoid tissue immune cells (macrophages, T cells)
protocol_notes: 1) Use non-permeabilized or mildly fixed cells and sections so that only surface or extracellular epitopes are probed. Run Duolink PLA with a mouse anti-B2M antibody and a rabbit anti-GPR82 antibody, after checking that the GPR82 antibody works. Check it on HEK293 cells overexpressing tagged GPR82 against parental cells, because GPCR antibodies are often poor. 2) Use HEK293 cells expressing epitope-tagged GPR82 (e.g. HA-GPR82) as a clean system, and run PLA with anti-tag plus anti-B2M. Test the effect of adding recombinant B2M. 3) Counter-stain with anti-HLA-ABC and anti-FCGRT or anti-CD1B. Test whether the PLA signal depends on MHC-I heavy chains, using B2M-null cells with B2M reconstituted. 4) Quantify PLA puncta per cell by confocal imaging in at least 3 biological replicates. If PLA is positive, confirm by co-IP of tagged GPR82 and B2M.
controls: Positive: a known surface pair, such as B2M with HLA-A/HLA-B heavy chain, in the same cells (PLA positive control). Negative: single-antibody PLA controls, GPR82-knockout or parental HEK293 cells (no GPR82), an unrelated tagged GPCR with B2M, and a B2M-knockout line. An isotype-matched antibody control is also needed.
caveats: Confidence is low: ipTM is 0.51, interface pLDDT is 64.9 and min PAE is 9.3 Å. B2M is nearly always bound to MHC-I-like heavy chains, so a positive PLA signal may reflect nearby MHC-I (a bystander, or an indirect link) instead of a direct B2M–GPR82 contact. It was not checked whether the GPR82 interface is extracellular or lies in a transmembrane or intracellular region, or whether it includes N-glycosylation sites, so it may be inaccessible or glycan-shielded. HPA gives no GPR82 subcellular or protein-level data, and the RNA is low except in Kupffer cells. GPR82 antibody quality is a main risk. PLA only shows proximity of about 40 nm, not a direct interaction or functional effect.

method_rationale: Both are plasma-membrane 7TM GPCRs expected in the same membrane, so a lateral heteromer is best tested by in situ proximity (<40 nm) in intact cells. PLA avoids detergent solubilisation, which often creates or destroys GPCR aggregates in co-IP. There is no known ligand pairing, so a stimulation assay has no obvious readout.
tissue_rationale: HPA lists brain as the only tissue-enriched site for both: ADORA1 at 42.6 nTPM and GPR62 at 22.8 nTPM. Single-cell data do not overlap (ADORA1 in podocytes at 142 nCPM, GPR62 in oligodendrocytes at 29.5 nCPM), so brain regions where oligodendrocyte-lineage cells and ADORA1-positive neurons/glia sit close together are the best tissue targets. Cell-level co-expression must be confirmed first.
protocol_notes: 1) First run RT-qPCR or RNAscope for ADORA1 and GPR62 in human or mouse brain sections and in primary oligodendrocyte/OPC cultures, to find cells that express both. 2) Use a heterologous system as the main test: HEK293 cells transfected with tagged ADORA1 and GPR62 (HA/FLAG), with PLA on non-permeabilised cells using anti-tag antibodies, so only surface pairs are detected. Then do endogenous PLA on PFA-fixed brain sections or primary oligodendrocytes with validated antibodies from different host species. 3) Quantify PLA puncta per cell by confocal imaging. Optionally add MTNR1B co-expression, because UniProt reports GPR62 heteromerising with MTNR1B, to see whether the signal changes in a three-way complex. 4) Optionally follow up with an ADORA1 agonist (CPA) or antagonist (DPCPX) and a cAMP readout, to see whether GPR62 modulates ADORA1 Gi signalling.
controls: Positive: a known GPCR heteromer pair, such as ADORA1–P2Y1 or ADORA1–A2A, or GPR62–MTNR1B if antibodies are available. Negative: a single-antibody PLA, cells expressing only one receptor, a non-interacting membrane protein of similar abundance (e.g. ADORA1 + an unrelated 7TM receptor or CD8-tagged construct), and, where possible, GPR62 knockout or siRNA knockdown to confirm the endogenous signal.
caveats: Confidence is low: ipTM is about 0.5, and AF3 packing of two 7TM bundles without a lipid bilayer often produces non-specific interfaces. HPA shows no shared cell type (ADORA1 podocytes vs GPR62 oligodendrocytes), so the two may never meet in the same cell in vivo. GPR62 has no HPA localisation data and no validated antibodies, so epitope-tagged constructs may be needed, and overexpression can cause artefactual proximity. PLA shows proximity, not a direct interaction. Because GPCRs are densely packed in membranes, PLA positives need the negative-control receptors above.

method_variant: Recombinant PPIA +/- BSG co-expression and +/- PNGase F / glycosylation-site mutant GPR63 arm
method_rationale: PPIA is a secreted protein and GPR63 is an orphan plasma-membrane GPCR, so this is a ligand-receptor hypothesis. A functional signalling readout (rather than proximity) tests whether PPIA actually engages and activates GPR63. Because PPIA is so abundant and sticky, binding alone would be hard to interpret.
tissue_rationale: HPA gives no tissue-level overlap for the pair. PPIA is highest in gastric progenitor cells (nCPM ~3194) and is annotated as secreted to blood. GPR63 is enriched only in choroid plexus epithelial cells (nCPM ~115.8), so the pair is paracrine/endocrine, and the assay is run in engineered cells plus a choroid plexus-derived model. Any in vivo overlap would be through circulating or CSF PPIA.
protocol_notes: 1) Express GPR63 (tagged, e.g. N-terminal HA/FLAG, with surface expression confirmed by flow or ELISA) in HEK293 cells, with and without BSG/CD147 co-expression. Use mock-transfected cells and a parallel BSG-only line as controls. Also test a choroid plexus epithelial line (e.g. HIBCPP or Z310) for endogenous GPR63. 2) Stimulate with endotoxin-free recombinant human PPIA (dose range 1 nM to 1 µM, 5 to 60 min). Read out GPCR signalling in G-protein-agnostic ways: cAMP (GloSensor/HTRF, because GPR63 is reported to couple Gi/Gs/G12-type pathways), β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter/NanoBiT), and SRE/NFAT/CRE reporters, plus pERK as the CD147 pathway readout. 3) Confirm direct binding with a orthogonal check: biotin-PPIA or His-PPIA pulldown from GPR63-expressing membranes, or a NanoBiT/BRET binding assay. Test cyclosporin A (a PPIA active-site inhibitor) and enzyme-dead PPIA R55A to see whether activity depends on the PPIase site. 4) Run the glycosylation arm in parallel: PNGase F or tunicamycin pretreatment, and N-to-Q mutants of the 3 predicted GPR63 N-glycosylation sites.
controls: Positive: a known GPCR agonist for assay validity (e.g. forskolin for cAMP, or a reference receptor/ligand pair in the same cells) and PPIA-induced pERK in BSG-expressing cells (established CD147 axis). Negative: mock-transfected or empty-vector cells, heat-denatured PPIA, an unrelated cyclophilin (PPIB) or irrelevant protein at the same concentration, an unrelated GPCR expressed at similar levels, and GPR63 knockout or knockdown in the choroid plexus line.
caveats: Confidence is low: ipTM is 0.5, only at threshold, and PPIA is a hub with 195 known interactors, so nonspecific stickiness is plausible. GPR63 has 3 unmodeled N-glycosylation sites, and their position relative to the predicted interface was not checked. A glycan could block or alter the interface, so the glycosidase and N-to-Q mutant arm is needed to interpret negative results. Any PPIA effect may be mediated by endogenous BSG/CD147 rather than GPR63, so BSG controls and GPR63 knockout are essential. GPR63 is an orphan receptor with no validated agonist or coupling assay, so the readout is uncertain. HPA also lists GPR63 in the nucleoplasm and cytosol as well as at the plasma membrane, so surface expression must be verified. HPA provides no tissue overlap, so physiological relevance is untested. Recombinant PPIA can carry endotoxin or tag artifacts.
